articles.content:
A number of people have been complaining that the new Siri demos during the keynote videos were a little on the slow side. There were notable lags of several seconds between Siri requests and the task being carried out.

But while the ideal we’re aiming for is for AI tasks to be carried out as quickly as possible, what we saw is kind of good news …

Apple was roundly criticised back in 2024 for using concept videos of features it was unable to demo.

What Apple showed regarding the upcoming “personalized Siri” at WWDC was not a demo. It was a concept video. Concept videos are bullshit, and a sign of a company in disarray, if not crisis.

That criticism was deserved, and Apple admitted that things were going to take longer than expected, deleted the offending video, and settled a $250M false advertising lawsuit.

The company seems to have learned its lesson. While the keynote wasn’t live, it does appear that all of the video demonstrations were conducted in real time, as TechCrunch noted.

Many of the Apple Intelligence demoes featured someone standing, phone in hand, pressing buttons or using voice commands in real time, while another camera showed off the phone’s response. These weren’t live onstage, anything-could-go wrong demos; they were pre-taped. But they looked far more like proof of working features than what Apple showed at WWDC 2024.

Indeed, John Gruber observed that there weren’t even any cuts between individual demos.

The demos were all shot in single takes, with no editing. In fact, I think most of them were single takes of multiple demos back-to-back.

What Apple showed off, then, appears to be a genuine reflection of how the new AI features work today. Joz actually says that because the demos were filmed a little ahead of WWDC, they were carried out with an older version of Siri AI, and it’s faster now:

We actually filmed these a bit in advance, that was Siri AI where it was at that point. You ask those same questions to it now, it’ll be faster, and at launch it will be faster still.

articles.title: Netflix's New 26-Minute GTA 6 Release Is Already the No. 1 Movie on Streaming
articles.subtitle: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto journey reaches Taylor Swift level We may never know who paid who in the Netflix-Rockstar deal that brought 26 minutes of carefully edited Grand Theft Auto 6 PlayStation 5 gameplay footage to the streaming platform (or for how...
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto journey reaches Taylor Swift level

We may never know who paid who in the Netflix-Rockstar deal that brought 26 minutes of carefully edited Grand Theft Auto 6 PlayStation 5 gameplay footage to the streaming platform (or for how much… but I bet it was a lot). What we do know is that the plan worked: Rockstar wanted to eventize the release of a trailer that would resonate with longtime fans — or perhaps dormant gamers nostalgic for GTA — and Netflix wanted the explosion of subscriptions, even in the short term.

The unique offer has, almost inevitably, skyrocketed to the top of Netflix charts on Friday. Less than 12 hours after its debut, the extended preview of the Lucia and Jason’s Vice City adventure was the number one movie on Netflix, besting legit “Recently Added” movies. Reports suggest that the premiere led to a full 50 percent bump in U.S. viewership on the platform.

And with that, in my opinion, GTA 6 has officially achieved Taylor Swift status.

Why owning Netflix feels like a big deal

When I say GTA 6 achieved Taylor Swift status, I don’t mean Taylor Swift the person, but “a Taylor Swift” as a cultural phenomenon — something so massive, so rare, and so anticipated that it can temporarily bend the rest of popular culture around itself.

Allow me to present this very specific chart of popularity as it pertains to Taylor Swift.

While not as powerful as a Literal Taylor Swift Thing, events like the World Cup, the Olympics, the biggest Marvel movies at their peak, and now more than ever, Christopher Nolan movies that become unavoidable months before they exist, all fit this description to a degree. GTA 6 has spent 13 years becoming that kind of thing, but the Netflix deal made its status newly legible outside the usual language of video game hype.

The similarities with Swift are striking. Both have turned scarcity into a form of power. Swift is famously selective about what she reveals and when; Rockstar has spent years maintaining an almost absurdly controlled information vacuum around GTA 6. Every scrap becomes an object of scrutiny. Fans dissect trailers, screenshots, release dates, social posts, and even incidental details for clues about what comes next.

The important thing is that the audience has become part of the marketing machine. Rockstar doesn’t need to constantly tell people to care about GTA 6 because millions of people are already doing the work of keeping it alive. They’re theorizing, arguing, making memes, producing fan art, and counting down to the next glimpse. The less Rockstar gives them, the more intensely they look.

Even people who don’t like the thing can contribute to its cultural dominance. You don’t have to be a GTA fan to know that GTA 6 exists or that it has been delayed, that everyone is waiting for it, or that its next trailer is a news event. Criticism and skepticism only add fuel to the conversation fire — nothing can smolder it.

The same phenomenon has made Swift difficult to escape: Her fans amplify her, her detractors amplify her, and mainstream institutions amplify both groups by covering the fight. Cultural saturation becomes the story.

The inevitable next milestone (not hands-on gameplay)

So the Netflix premiere, and its embrace by subscribers, is notable. Rockstar did not need Netflix to sell GTA 6; the game had already generated enormous demand from a handful of trailers and years of almost total secrecy. But Netflix wanted the cultural gravity of GTA 6 badly enough to make an unusual arrangement around it.

There’s a useful precedent in the Eras Tour. Taylor Swift didn’t need Disney Plus to make the tour successful; the tour was already one of the biggest cultural phenomena on the planet, and she released her own concert movie by way of AMC Theatres. Yet Disney paid an enormous premium to bring the concert film to its streaming service, effectively buying into the cultural gravity Swift had created rather than creating it for her. Netflix’s relationship with GTA 6 feels like a similar transaction.

That’s the Taylor Swift (designation, not person) threshold: when the biggest institutions and brands around you begin rearranging themselves to accommodate your arrival. GTA 6 has been culturally enormous for years, but the Netflix premiere demonstrated that its power now extends beyond the boundaries of gaming.

And everyone wants a piece of the pie. On Thursday night, Rockstar seized control of Netflix, The New York Times, and by 9 p.m. EDT, the YouTube economy. Fans, doing the work for Rockstar, already had Spotify wallpapered with playlists to round up all of GTA 6's needle drops.

There are still many unanswered questions coming off the Netflix GTA 6 footage — about gameplay, about the online possibilities. But the only one I really have: When will Rockstar ship Travis Kelce an early copy so Taylor Swift can snap a pic of him for Instagram while she’s recording a sequel song to “So High School”? Even a titan like T. Swift may want to leverage the power of this game before it drops on Nov. 19.

articles.title: The MacRumors Show: Apple's Surprisingly Big Week of Announcements
articles.subtitle: It's been an unusually big week for Apple announcements. On this week's episode of The MacRumors Show, we discuss the new Mac mini and Mac Studio, the M6 and M5 Ultra chips, and invites to Apple's September event.
articles.author: MacRumors
articles.content:
It's been an unusually big week for Apple announcements. On this week's episode of The MacRumors Show, we discuss the new Mac mini and Mac Studio, the M6 and M5 Ultra chips, and invites to Apple's September event.

Apple announced the new Mac mini on Tuesday, offering M6 and M5 Pro chip options. The machine gains an N1 networking chip, bringing Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and moves to 2. 5Gb Ethernet as standard, up from 1Gb, with a 10Gb option. Thunderbolt 5 is restricted to the M5 Pro model, which gets three Thunderbolt 5 ports while the M6 model keeps Thunderbolt 4.

Genlock support over USB-C also helps to sync a display's refresh timing to a camera such as the iPhone 17 Pro. Pricing starts at $899 with 16GB and 256GB, rising to $1,699 for the M5 Pro at 24GB and 512GB. Pre-orders are now open, with launch on September 22.

The M6 is Apple's first 2nm chip. Its 12-core CPU is split into 2 super cores, 4 performance cores and 6 efficiency cores, making it the first Apple chip to combine all three core types in one design. Super cores are Apple's top tier, optimized for single-threaded speed. The 12-core GPU features a Neural Accelerator in each core for the first time in a ‌Mac mini‌.

The GPU also adds an updated shader architecture, Dynamic Caching, and hardware-accelerated ray tracing, while an all-new Dual 16-core Neural Engine doubles peak compute over the previous generation, with system frameworks able to drive both engines at once. Memory starts at 16GB and tops out at 32GB, running at up to 170GB/s. M5 Pro scales further, to an 18-core CPU, a 20-core GPU and up to 64GB at 307GB/s.

The new Mac Studio arrived alongside the ‌Mac mini‌, with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chip options. The M5 Max offers an 18-core CPU with 6 super cores and 12 performance cores, an up-to-40-core GPU with Neural Accelerators in every core, and up to 128GB of memory at 614GB/s, with the GPU running up to 50% faster than the previous generation.

Both configurations move to a next-generation SSD architecture on PCIe Gen 6 for up to twice the storage performance, and gain up to six Thunderbolt 5 ports at 120Gb/s, and the same genlock support as the ‌Mac mini‌. Apple's N1 chip also brings Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 to the ‌Mac Studio‌.

Pricing starts at $2,499 for the M5 Max at 36GB and 512GB, and $5,499 for the M5 Ultra at 96GB and 1TB, with the 512GB memory option not arriving until late October.

The M5 Ultra is Apple's first quad-die chip, using a next-generation version of UltraFusion to join two dual-die M5 Max chips into a single processor. The result is a CPU with up to 36 cores, 12 super and 24 performance, delivering 1. 25x the single-threaded and 1. 3x the multithreaded performance of the M3 Ultra.

Its up-to-80-core GPU is the most powerful Apple silicon GPU ever made and the first on an Ultra chip to feature Neural Accelerators. Second-generation Dynamic Caching, hardware-accelerated mesh shading and third-generation ray tracing lift graphics up 40% over the M3 Ultra, and the chip features a 32-core Neural Engine. Memory reaches 512GB at 1. 2TB/s, which is a 50% bandwidth increase.

Other announcements this week included a new, softer Apple Polishing Cloth at $9, down from $19, and refreshed U.S. Magic Keyboards for the Mac, now featuring glyphs instead of edge text. Apple Support's 1-800-APL-CARE line is also now answered by a generative AI assistant in the U.S. and Canada.

articles.title: Apple unveils M6, M5 Ultra chips and updates its desktop Macs
articles.subtitle: In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers.…
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
In a bit of a late-August surprise while the world awaits word on the next generation of iPhones, on Tuesday Apple announced two new processors, the M5 Ultra and M6, which help power new iterations of its Mac Studio and Mac mini desktop computers. Both models are available to pre-order now and will ship on September 22 and will run macOS 27 Golden Gate.

Bridging the generations

The M6 chip kicks off Apple’s next chip generation, and is its first based on a 2-nanometer production process. It’s also got the first 12-core CPU in Apple’s base M-series chip line, up from 10 cores in the M4 and M5 generations.

Those CPU cores are in an interesting configuration: The M6 is the first Apple chip to mix all three of its CPU core types. The chip has six efficiency cores, four performance cores, and two super cores.

According to Apple, each core design is focused on a different primary task: efficiency cores are meant to sip power (useful when running simple background tasks); performance cores are optimized for complex, multi-threaded jobs; and super cores were created to offer the highest possible single-threaded performance.

Apple claims that this design results in record-setting single-threaded performance and up to 1.2x speed improvements over the M5 chip. The M6 also offers a dual 16-core Neural Engine, for on-device AI performance. Memory bandwidth peaks at 170GB/s, 10 percent faster than the M5.

Just as the new chip generation arrives, the previous one ( launched in October 2025 ) is completed. The M5 Ultra is Apple’s first new Ultra chip since it introduced the M3 Ultra in March 2025. Apple says it’s using the next generation of its UltraFusion technology to connect two dual-die M5 Max chips to make Apple silicon’s first quad-die chip. UltraFusion connects the two dies with bandwidth of more than 4.4TB/s, letting the four dies work as a single chip.

The M5 Ultra offers up to 36 CPU cores (12 super/24 performance), which Apple says results in up to 1.25x higher single-threaded performance and up to 1.3x higher multithreaded performance than the M3 Ultra. It offers up to 80 GPU cores and up to 512GB of memory with 1.2TB/s of unified memory bandwidth.

Meet the Mac mini

Previously available in M4 and M4 Pro configurations, the new Mac mini is available in M6 and M5 Pro chip options. The new base price is $899, up $100 from the previous base, for the same standard 16GB RAM/256GB storage configuration. The M5 Pro configuration starts at $1699, also up $100 from the model sold until Tuesday.

(But keep in mind, the M4 Mac mini was introduced at $599 before Apple recently raised that price. Put together, it’s a 50% price increase over the model introduced almost two years ago. We all know why, but it still hurts. )

Because the Mac mini previously shipped with M4 processors, this new model picks up numerous improvements Apple made in the M5 generation, including GPUs better optimized for AI performance. Both models support Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 chip, and 2.5Gb Ethernet is now standard, with 10Gb Ethernet still available as an add-on. The M6 model supports Thunderbolt 4, but the M5 Pro model supports Thunderbolt 5.

Mac Studio advances in unison

At the same moment the Mac mini becomes split between two chip generations, the Mac Studio gets reunified with chips from the same generation: the M5 Max and the new M5 Ultra. As mentioned previously, the M5 Ultra is basically two M5 Max chips connected together by Apple’s dense, fast UltraFusion technology. Apple boasts that the M5 Ultra is the fastest chip Apple has ever created, which isn’t much of a stretch since the M5 Max was already pretty far up there.

The Mac Studio is effectively the replacement for the Mac Pro, and it’s alone in offering the Ultra-class chip. Apple has positioned the Mac Studio as ideal for local AI workflows, and the new models will still be able to cluster via Thunderbolt 5 to create even larger collections of memory and performance.

Apple representatives pointed out that a four-Mac Studio AI cluster, like the one I saw on display at WWDC earlier this summer, is so efficient that it can be powered from a single standard wall outlet. (They even showed us a picture of four Mac Studios plugged into a power strip that was plugged into the wall.

) In an era of data center excesses, Apple is clearly leaning into the possibility of small, efficient Macs being used to do local AI work rather than relying on huge, power-hungry cloud models.

As with the Mac mini, the Mac Studio gains M5 chip improvements that benefit AI models running on GPU cores, integrate the N1 chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6, and support 2x faster storage with speeds up to 15GB/s.

articles.title: The Utility App Flood Won’t Last
articles.subtitle: The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.
articles.author: MacStories
articles.content:
The App Store is evolving at a breakneck pace not seen since its earliest days. We saw the first glimmers of what was to come early in 2025, but it wasn’t until late last year that the tsunami of apps developed with the help of AI agents really took hold.

Since then, veteran developers are releasing new apps and updating existing ones faster than ever, and new developers are releasing their first apps in droves. Today, supply is dramatically up, demand is flat, and quality is seemingly simultaneously up and down, depending on where you look.

How these forces play out long-term is anyone’s guess, but it’s worth examining because, just as Federico’s link to Bryan Irace’s post about agentic coding tools foreshadowed the rise of tools like Codex and Claude Code, today’s trends are sparks that have the potential to become tomorrow’s App Store wildfires or simply fizzle out.

Utility apps are on the front lines of this change. The TechCrunch story I linked in April picked up on this trend:

Another interesting tidbit from Appfigures is that the Utilities app category moved up the top five chart.

If anything, the trend has accelerated in the months since.

It’s not surprising at all that utility apps have taken off. They’ve been a staple of new developers since long before agents came along. That’s because many are UI wrappers around command line tools. That isn’t a knock against the developers of those apps; most users don’t want to open Terminal to convert a video or audio file to another format using ffmpeg, for example. By building a great UI around command line tools, developers have made them far easier to use.

However, the relative simplicity and narrow scope of many utility apps have made them a natural fit for AI agents, too. That’s why the App Store (and my inbox) is deluged with Mac menu bar and single-screen iPhone and iPad utility apps.

On the one hand, the abundance of utilities has been great for users. More choice means you’re more likely to find the app that perfectly fits your needs.

On the other hand, though, I don’t think what’s happening in the category is sustainable and expect to see it dramatically shift again in the coming months. As we’ve seen from reporting by The New York Times, app supply is outstripping demand by orders of magnitude, which will drive down prices. That alone is likely to cause the utility app market to shrink. But there’s more to it than that.

Remember, the demand shifts that The New York Times reported, based on Sensor Tower numbers, are for the entire App Store, where download numbers have grown 2-3% this year and last. I expect utility downloads to actually shrink in the coming months – again, because of agents.

Utilities, especially simple ones, are exactly the sorts of apps that are becoming trivially easy for power users – the very users these utilities are made for – to create themselves. From frontier labs‘ model improvements to a growing number of app-building tools from those same labs and third parties, it’s never been easier to build a web or native app yourself.

And although I agree with people, like Nilay Patel, who say the notion that everyone will build their own software is overblown, the utility market is different. Your average person is not downloading apps to adjust the frame rate and file format of a video or downloading YouTube videos to watch later.

But those are exactly the sort of things that people who are using agents are doing with them, whether they’re having an agent do those things directly via a command line tool in an app like Codex or Claude Code or building an app to do the same thing. That’s going to put even more pressure on the category.

That said, I think there will always be a cohort of users who would rather pay for an app than build it themselves, so I’m not predicting the demise of utilities in general – just the end of today’s frothy market. I also think there remains a place for simple utilities that solve hard problems with clever solutions. Not every utility is a UI wrapper for a terminal command. Plenty of apps feature original solutions or thoughtful and unconventional remixes of disparate tools.

Utilities aren’t going away, but just like other App Store deluges, the trend will recede. It’s just that this time, it’s likely to flip faster than usual.

Yahoo Finance was one of those to attribute the slide to the WWDC announcements.

Siri AI will launch in beta later this year for supported devices set to English and will not be available initially in the European Union on iOS or iPadOS. articles.title: Pokémon Officially Returns to Galar for New Disney+ Series in 2027
articles.subtitle: Finally, a real look at Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch’d & Pichu Disney and Pokémon are teaming up for a new streaming series coming to Disney Plus in 2027.
articles.author: Polygon
articles.content:
Finally, a real look at Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch’d & Pichu

Disney and Pokémon are teaming up for a new streaming series coming to Disney Plus in 2027. Disney and The Pokémon Company announced Friday that the stop-motion animated adventure series Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd & Pichu is now slated to debut on Disney XD and to stream exclusively on Disney Plus in 2027. A new trailer for the show was also released on Friday as part of the Pokémon XP event happening in San Francisco this weekend.

The announcement of The Misadventures of Sirfetch’d & Pichu is part of a bigger push to bring Pokémon to Disney Plus.

What is Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd & Pichu?

Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd & Pichu is a brand-new series from Aardman Animations, the creators of Wallace & Gromit, Chicken Run, and Shaun the Sheep. The series will focus on Sirfetch'd and Pichu as they journey through Pokémon Sword and Shield 's Galar region on heroic and friendly adventures. Here's the show's official synopsis:

In “Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd & Pichu,” Sirfetch'd and Pichu embark on an epic journey through the Galar Region. Together, they set out on a gallant quest to help and protect Pokémon across the region. Their missions rarely go as planned, but their noble deeds forge their friendship as they step bravely into the unknown where peril, alliances, rivalries, extraordinary Pokémon, and endless laughs await them.

Image: Aardman Animations/The Pokémon Company

Aardman's collaboration with Pokémon was originally announced in 2024. Sean Clarke, managing director of Aardman, said at the time, “Bringing together Pokémon, the world’s biggest entertainment brand, together with our love of craft, character and comedic storytelling feels incredibly exciting.

Aardman and [The Pokémon Company] share an emphasis on heritage and attention to detail as well as putting our fans and audiences at the heart of what we do, which we know will steer us right as we together create charming, original and new stories for audiences around the world. ”

Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch’d & Pichu will debut on Disney XD and stream on Disney Plus sometime in 2027.

Pokémon officially has a new streaming home

Pokémon the Series: The Beginning, the classic Pokémon anime, is also now on Disney Plus in the U.S. and select international markets. Season 1 of the Pokémon anime series is now streaming on Disney Plus alongside later seasons available via Hulu: Pokémon the Series: Sun & Moon (season 20), Pokémon the Series: Sun & Moon Ultra Adventures (season 21), and Pokémon the Series: Sun & Moon Ultra Legends (season 22).

“Pokémon has that rare ability to mean something to longtime fans while continuing to feel completely relevant to young audiences today,” said Ayo Davis, president of Disney Kids & Family.

“This new series ‘ Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd & Pichu ’ brings Aardman’s signature stop-motion artistry with a bold, playful new perspective to this beloved world, giving audiences a fresh way to experience the characters they know and love. Along with ‘ Pokémon the Series: The Beginning,’ these series are powerful additions to Disney XD and Disney+. ”

“These stories, full of adventure and heroism, all told from the perspective of Pokémon is made even more exciting through the lens of the incredible filmmakers at Aardman,” said Pokémon director of original animation Phil Rynda. “Audiences will be delighted getting to know the Sirfetch'd & Pichu, and wonderful cast of Pokémon, featured in this series.

Aardman has brought Galar to life in a way that makes you feel like you can smell the air, touch the tree bark, and want to adventure alongside our series heroes. ”

Apple is updating how digital purchases cost money in a few parts of the world. The company shared that new tax rules and currency shifts are causing it to tweak pricing on the App Store in several regions. These adjustments impact things like paid software and in-app buys, though not every single purchase will see a shift in cost right away. People who build software for the tech giant will notice these updates rolling out in phases over the coming weeks as storefronts adjust to new regional rules.

Tax updates impact developer payouts in three countries today

Starting immediately, the money developers take home from sales is changing in three places. This happens because local governments are rolling out new tax laws. Morocco is bringing in a new value-added tax of 20 percent. The Republic of the Congo is doing something similar by adding an 18 percent value-added tax.

On top of that, Tanzania is bumping up its digital sales tax. That specific rate is moving from 2 percent to 3 percent. These early updates just change how much money developers keep after a sale, not the price buyers see on the screen.

App prices shift across four storefronts starting in mid-September

If you pay for something that renews automatically every month, those subscription costs are not changing. Prices also stay put if a developer handles regional pricing manually instead of letting the platform do it automatically.

These routine tweaks happen pretty often as economies shift. It is common for Apple to update its global pricing to keep up with changing local taxes and currency values, making sure the digital market stays balanced across borders.

articles.title: App Report: Easy listening, easier reading
articles.subtitle: We’ve got a pair of apps that help you get a little reading done, albeit with two different approaches. Still, whether you prefer having someone else read the articles to you or if you just prefer a cleaner feed of articles, there’s something for everyone...
articles.author: Six Colors
articles.content:
We’ve got a pair of apps that help you get a little reading done, albeit with two different approaches. Still, whether you prefer having someone else read the articles to you or if you just prefer a cleaner feed of articles, there’s something for everyone in this week’s App Report.

If there’s something you think belongs in our weekly look at promising macOS and iOS apps, just drop us a line at apps@sixcolors.com with a brief description of the app in question. We can’t reply to every email we get, but we’ll certainly take a look at any and all apps for a future column.

Listen Later

Six Colors readers may be familiar with Listen Later, which has provided a way to turn articles you’ve been meaning to read into podcasts that you can listen to at your convenience. Recently, there’s been an expansion in the ways you can access the service, with both an iOS app and a Safari extension giving you new ways to send URLs and PDFs to Listen Later so that they can be converted into a podcast.

In the iOS version of Listen Later, a Submit tab offers a field for pasting text, HTML or links; there’s also an optional button for uploading PDFs to the service. I’m able to link Listen Later to my podcatcher of choice — in this case, it’s Overcast — and a new episode featuring the content I’ve submitted shows up in my feed after it’s been converted to audio form.

The Safari extension for macOS works much the same way, only there’s a button next to the search/URL field that I tap when I want to submit something to Listen Later.

Both the Listen Later iOS app and Safari extension for macOS are free downloads, with $2 in credits for new users. If you like what you hear, you’ll need to purchase additional credits through Listen Later to cover the cost of AI processing and audio generation.

PageFeed

Reading articles on your iPhone can be a delight, but scrolling from the start of the article to the end can take some of the pleasure out of the process. If that’s a problem for you, PageFeed comes to the rescue by adopting a more book-like format for a news reader. Instead of scrolling, you tap to turn the page to make your way through an article.

The idea, PageFeed developer Brad Moss says in the description for the iOS app, is to add some degree of calm to reading through your news feed. You can select the sources and topics you want to read about. A share sheet can also send articles you find elsewhere to PageFeed for a scrolling-free experience.

You can download the app to your iPhone or iPad for free and use it for 14 days to get a feel for PageFeed’s approach. After that, a one-time $10 fee unlocks the app for good.

Tansei

It would be unfair to describe Tansei as kind of a universal clipboard for your Mac, even if that’s what this utility does, at least in a broad sense. But Tansei is really a storage space for anything. Besides text and URLs, it can hold images, screenshots and even colors, keeping them in a shelf on the side of your display for you to access whenever you need.

In my testing, Tansei has already proven its worth for a weekly newsletter I put together every week. I include a lot of links in that newsletter, and previously, that meant keeping an open text document where I could copy down URLs to articles of interest for use when it came time to put a new issue together.

With Tansei running on my Mac, all I have to do is copy the URL, and it shows up in Tansei’s shelf automatically. I can also drag-and-drop items into Tansei, and hide the app off to the side when I want an uncluttered screen.

I wish there was a way to exert a little more control over what gets copied. For example, while moving the newsletter text into the publishing site I use, every block of text I copy over appears in Tansei. At least the app offers a bulk management feature that I can use to delete unnecessary items in one fell swoop.

You can buy Tansei for a one-time payment of $7, though a three-day trial lets you use the app for free without restrictions.

articles.title: MacPaw is building an on-device AI layer that will work across your Mac apps
articles.subtitle: MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac. The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.
articles.author: 9to5Mac Apps
articles.content:
MacPaw has announced a long-term strategic partnership with Liquid AI to co-develop an on-device AI technology stack built specifically for the Mac.

The collaboration will start with Eney, MacPaw’s AI assistant for macOS.

MacPaw is teaming up with Liquid AI to bring more on-device AI to the Mac

Liquid AI’s Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) will be adapted for Mac-based assistance and combined with MacPaw’s own on-device technologies: Mnemos for memory and Elix for inference.

Eney already shifted to a local model last year, keeping reasoning, contextual search, skill execution, and conversation history on the device whenever possible.

The new partnership is intended to push that approach further. The two companies are jointly developing the underlying stack rather than MacPaw simply adding another third-party model.

Once the technology has been tested and implemented in Eney, MacPaw says it plans to bring it to more of its products. It also wants to make the shared AI stack available to Mac developers through Setapp.

That could let participating apps expose more of their capabilities and context to Eney. This would allow the assistant to understand what is inside an app. It could also provide more useful answers or take relevant actions.

You can learn more about MacPaw’s on-device AI technology and today’s announcement here, and catch up on Liquid AI here.
